title: Why Doctors Were Ordered to Wash Their Hands
topic: Ignaz Semmelweis and why doctors in 1847 Vienna were ordered to wash their hands (childbed fever)

lines: A doctor scrubbed his hands in lime bleach before touching new mothers.
It was 1847, and childbed fever was killing mothers in hospitals.
Some doctors mocked Semmelweis for demanding clean hands.
Other doctors felt the request insulted their status as gentlemen.
Women begged on their knees to avoid his ward.
Some women gave birth in the streets to escape it.
In May 1847, Semmelweis ordered hand washing in the First Division.
Every doctor and student washed before ward work.
Semmelweis later ordered washing before each vaginal examination.
The First Division death rate fell from 18% to less than 3%.
You see, it is like cleaning a kitchen after a greasy meal.
Doctors in the First Division performed autopsies each morning.
Second Division midwives did no autopsies, and their death rate stayed low.
Semmelweis believed corpse particles stuck to doctors' hands and spread childbed fever.
Chlorinated lime, a strong cleaning solution, washed those particles away.
Semmelweis's ideas were accepted only after his death.
Louis Pasteur later confirmed that germs cause disease.
His colleagues committed him to an asylum, where guards beat him.
The man who demanded clean hands died from a rotting hand wound.
